Combine pipelines

Source: vignettes/v03a-combine-pipelines.Rmd
v03a-combine-pipelines.Rmd

The possibility to combine pipelines basically allows to modularize the pipeline creation process. This is especially useful when you have a set of pipelines that are used in different contexts and you want to avoid code duplication1.

Two pipelines

Let’s define one pipeline that is used for data preprocessing and one that does the modelling2.

library(pipeflow)

pip1 <- pip_new("preprocess") |>
    pip_add("data", \(x = 1:5) x) |>
    pip_add("prep", \(x = ~data) x + 1) |>
    pip_add("standardize", \(x = ~prep, scale = 2) x * scale)
pip2 <- pip_new("model") |>
    pip_add("data", \(x = 1:5) x) |>
    pip_add("fit", \(x = ~data, k = 2, b = 0) x * k + b) |>
    pip_add("predict", \(x = ~fit) paste0("pred: ", x))

Combined pipeline

Next we combine the two pipelines using rbind().

pip <- rbind(pip1, pip2)

pip
# <pipeflow> preprocess-model (6 steps)
# -------------------------------------
#           step  params depends state
# 1:        data       x           new
# 2:        prep       x    data   new
# 3: standardize x,scale    prep   new
# 4:       data2       x           new
# 5:         fit   x,k,b   data2   new
# 6:     predict       x     fit   new
# -------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: never

Note that the data step of the second pipeline has been renamed to data2 in both the step and the depends columns (see line 4 above). That is, when “rbinding” pipelines, {pipeflow} automatically ensures that all step names stay unique by renaming any duplicates accordingly.

As is also visible from the graphical representation of the pipeline,

library(visNetwork)
do.call(visNetwork, args = pip_graph(pip)) |>
    visHierarchicalLayout(direction = "LR")

the two pipelines are not yet connected. To make sense of the combined pipeline, we want to use the output of the standardize step as the input of the data2 step, which we can do by applying the replace function, which was introduced in the previous vignette modify the pipeline, as follows:

pip |> pip_replace("data2", \(x = ~standardize) x)

pip
# <pipeflow> preprocess-model (6 steps)
# -------------------------------------
#           step  params     depends state
# 1:        data       x               new
# 2:        prep       x        data   new
# 3: standardize x,scale        prep   new
# 4:       data2       x standardize   new
# 5:         fit   x,k,b       data2   new
# 6:     predict       x         fit   new
# -------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: never

The data2 step points to the output of the standardize step, so that both pipelines are now connected.

Relative indexing

Since the name of the re-routed step might not always be known3, the {pipeflow} package also provides a relative position indexing mechanism, which allows to rewrite the above command using a number (instead of the step name standardize) while having the same effect as above.

pip |> pip_replace("data2", \(x = ~ -1) x)

pip
# <pipeflow> preprocess-model (6 steps)
# -------------------------------------
#           step  params     depends state
# 1:        data       x               new
# 2:        prep       x        data   new
# 3: standardize x,scale        prep   new
# 4:       data2       x standardize   new
# 5:         fit   x,k,b       data2   new
# 6:     predict       x         fit   new
# -------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: never

The relative indexing mechanism allows to refer to steps positioned above the current step. The index ~-1 can be interpreted as “go one step back”, ~-2 as “go two steps back”, and so on.

Binding params when combining

Instead of replacing the step afterwards, the two pipelines can also be connected right away with the bind argument of rbind(). It takes a named list of one-sided formulas, which binds unbound params of the second pipeline to steps of the first one:

pip_bound <- rbind(pip1, pip2, bind = list(x = ~standardize))

pip_bound
# <pipeflow> preprocess-model (6 steps)
# -------------------------------------
#           step  params     depends state
# 1:        data       x               new
# 2:        prep       x        data   new
# 3: standardize x,scale        prep   new
# 4:       data2       x standardize   new
# 5:         fit   x,k,b       data2   new
# 6:     predict       x         fit   new
# -------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: never

The param x of the data2 step now refers to the standardize step, as if it had been defined as \(x = ~standardize) x. The same holds for any other step of the second pipeline with an unbound param x. Steps where x already refers to another step, like fit and predict, are left as they are, and so are the steps of the first pipeline: the data step still has its param x. Steps are bound by name, not by relative position, and bind can only be used when combining exactly two pipelines.

Binding params afterwards

Params can also be bound after combining, with pip_set_params(): a one-sided formula binds the param to that step in all selected steps that have it unbound. Here the data step of the first pipeline has an unbound param x as well, but it comes before the standardize step, so it can’t be bound to it. Therefore, we select the data2 step with a view:

pip_later <- rbind(pip1, pip2)
pip_set_params(pip_later["data2"], list(x = ~standardize))

pip_later
# <pipeflow> preprocess-model (6 steps)
# -------------------------------------
#           step  params     depends state
# 1:        data       x               new
# 2:        prep       x        data   new
# 3: standardize x,scale        prep   new
# 4:       data2       x standardize   new
# 5:         fit   x,k,b       data2   new
# 6:     predict       x         fit   new
# -------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: never

Without the view, pip_set_params() would signal an error and leave the pipeline unchanged. Like with bind, the steps are bound by name, not by relative position.

Combined pipeline results

Let’s now run the combined pipeline and inspect the results of the final step.

pip_run(pip)
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.874 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'preprocess-model'
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.874 UTC]: Step 1/6 data
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.876 UTC]: Step 2/6 prep
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.877 UTC]: Step 3/6 standardize
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.878 UTC]: Step 4/6 data2
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.879 UTC]: Step 5/6 fit
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.880 UTC]: Step 6/6 predict
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:36.881 UTC]: Finished run of pipeflow 'preprocess-model'
pip[["predict", "out"]]
# [1] "pred: 8"  "pred: 12" "pred: 16" "pred: 20" "pred: 24"

As we can see, the outputs of the preprocessing pipeline flow into the modelling pipeline. We can now go ahead and for example change the multiplier of the fit step and rerun the pipeline.

pip_set_params(pip, params = list(k = 3))
pip_run(pip)
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.144 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'preprocess-model'
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.144 UTC]: Step 1/6 data - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.144 UTC]: Step 2/6 prep - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.144 UTC]: Step 3/6 standardize - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.144 UTC]: Step 4/6 data2 - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.144 UTC]: Step 5/6 fit
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.147 UTC]: Step 6/6 predict
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.149 UTC]: Finished run of pipeflow 'preprocess-model'
pip[["predict", "out"]]
# [1] "pred: 12" "pred: 18" "pred: 24" "pred: 30" "pred: 36"

Saving and restoring pipelines

A pipeline, like the combined one above, can be built once and reused later, also in another R session. To this end, it can be saved to a file with saveRDS() and read back with readRDS()4.

file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(pip, file)

pip_restored <- readRDS(file)
pip_restored
# <pipeflow> preprocess-model (6 steps)
# -------------------------------------
#           step  params     depends state                                          out
# 1:        data       x              done                                    1,2,3,4,5
# 2:        prep       x        data  done                                    2,3,4,5,6
# 3: standardize x,scale        prep  done                                4, 6, 8,10,12
# 4:       data2       x standardize  done                                4, 6, 8,10,12
# 5:         fit   x,k,b       data2  done                               12,18,24,30,36
# 6:     predict       x         fit  done pred: 12,pred: 18,pred: 24,pred: 30,pred: 36
# -------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-20 18:51:37

The restored pipeline has all steps, parameters, outputs and states of the saved one. That is, it can be modified and run right away, and only the steps that need an update are run again:

pip_set_params(pip_restored, params = list(k = 4))
pip_run(pip_restored)
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.346 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'preprocess-model'
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.346 UTC]: Step 1/6 data - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.346 UTC]: Step 2/6 prep - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.346 UTC]: Step 3/6 standardize - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.347 UTC]: Step 4/6 data2 - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.347 UTC]: Step 5/6 fit
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.348 UTC]: Step 6/6 predict
# info [2026-10-20 18:51:37.349 UTC]: Finished run of pipeflow 'preprocess-model'

pip_restored[["predict", "out"]]
# [1] "pred: 16" "pred: 24" "pred: 32" "pred: 40" "pred: 48"

Both the saved and the restored pipelines are independent of each other, so the original pip still uses the multiplier k = 3:

pip_get_params(pip)$k
# [1] 3

For more details see also the section “Saving pipelines” in the help of pip_new().

Whether you combine them or not, in practice pipelines can get long quickly. The next vignette shows how you can easily focus on certain parts of your entire analysis workflow by Pipeline views.
